title: Probability: Outcomes, Chance and Experiments
seo_title: Grade 6 Probability Worksheets with Answers (CAPS Maths)
standard_text: Perform simple repeated events and list possible outcomes for experiments such as tossing a coin, rolling a die and spinning a spinner; list possible outcomes for experiments; count and compare the frequency of actual outcomes for a series of trials up to 50 trials.
meta_desc: Free CAPS Grade 6 probability worksheets: the probability scale, outcomes, probability as a fraction, experiments and fair games. 100 questions with memos.
key_big: Probability = ways it can happen ÷ all outcomes.
body_html:
How to think about it

  • Probability shows how likely an event is, from impossible (0) to certain (1).
  • List all the possible outcomes. A dice has 6.
  • Probability = number of ways it can happen ÷ number of possible outcomes: rolling a 5 is 16.
  • In an experiment, the results are close to the prediction but not always the same.

Examples

Example

A bag has 3 red and 5 blue beads

8 beads, 3 red

Answer: P(red) = 3/8

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
All equally likelyCount the ways each can happen.
It is dueA coin has no memory.
Exact matchResults vary.

faq.q: What does CAPS Grade 6 say about probability?
faq.a: Perform simple repeated events, list possible outcomes, and count and compare the frequency of actual outcomes for a series of trials.

faq.q: What is the probability of a head?

faq.a: Each player has the same chance to win.

items.q: What is the probability of an event that is impossible?
items.e: An impossible event can never happen, so its probability is 0. 0,1 is very unlikely, but it can still happen.

items.q: What is the probability of an event that is certain?
items.e: A certain event will happen, so its probability is 1 (or 100%). The number 100 on its own is far bigger than 1, so it can’t be a probability.

items.q: What is the probability of an event with an even chance?
items.e: An even chance is halfway between 0 and 1: 12 (0,5 or 50%). 2 is the number of outcomes, not the probability.

items.q: Which number can NOT be a probability?
items.e: Probabilities go from 0 to 1. 1,5 is bigger than 1, so it can’t be a probability. 0 and 1 are allowed: they mean impossible and certain.

items.q: Which percentage can NOT be a probability?
items.e: As a percentage, probabilities go from 0% to 100%. 120% is more than 100%, so it is not possible.

items.q: Which word best describes the chance shown by the arrow?
items.e: The arrow is at 0,8. That is between 0,5 and 1, close to 1: likely. It is not certain, because it is not at 1.

items.q: Which word best describes the chance shown by the arrow?
items.e: The arrow is at 0,1, close to 0 but not at 0: unlikely. Impossible would be exactly 0.

items.q: Which probability means an event is very likely?
items.e: 0,95 is very close to 1, so the event is very likely. 0,05 is very close to 0 (very unlikely). 9,5 is bigger than 1, so it is not a probability.

items.q: Which probability shows the most likely event?
items.e: Compare the tenths: 0,8 = 0,80 is the biggest. 0,35 has more digits, but 0,35 < 0,80. So 0,8 is most likely.

items.q: Which probability shows the least likely event?
items.e: Write them with two decimal places: 0,05; 0,50; 0,15; 0,30. The smallest is 0,05, so that event is least likely.

items.q: You roll a normal six-sided dice. What is the probability of rolling a 7?
items.e: A normal dice only has 1 to 6, so a 7 is impossible. Its probability is 0.

items.q: You roll a normal six-sided dice. What is the probability of rolling a number from 1 to 6?
items.e: Every roll gives a number from 1 to 6, so it is certain: 1. 6 is the number of outcomes, and probabilities are never more than 1.

items.q: The scale is split into quarters. What probability does the arrow show?
items.e: There are 4 equal parts from 0 to 1, and the arrow is 1 part from 0: 14 (0,25). 34 counts from the 1 end. 14 is 0,25, not 0,4.

items.q: The scale is split into tenths. What probability does the arrow show?
items.e: Each small step is 0,1. The arrow is 7 steps from 0, so it shows 0,7. 0,3 counts back from 1. 7 is too big to be a probability.

items.q: What is the probability shown by the arrow, as a percentage?
items.e: The arrow is at 0,3. 0,3 = 30 hundredths = 30%. 3% would be 0,03.

items.q:
Which list orders these probabilities from least likely to most likely?
0,6; 0,25; 0,9; 0,06
items.e: Write them as hundredths: 0,60; 0,25; 0,90; 0,06. Smallest to largest: 0,06; 0,25; 0,6; 0,9. 0,25 is less than 0,6, even though 25 is more than 6.

items.q: A bag has 3 red and 7 blue marbles. You take one without looking. Which letter shows the probability of taking a red marble?
items.e: 3 of the 10 marbles are red: 310 = 0,3. That is point B. C (0,7) is the probability of blue.

items.q: A spinner has 10 equal sections: 7 green and 3 yellow. Which letter shows the probability of landing on green?
items.e: 7 of the 10 equal sections are green: 710 = 0,7. That is point C.

items.q: An event is equally likely to happen or not happen. What is its probability?
items.e: Equally likely is halfway between 0 and 1: 12 (0,5 or 50%). 2 is the number of outcomes, not the probability.

items.q: Which percent can NOT be a probability?
items.e: As a percent, probabilities go from 0% to 100%. 120% is more than 100%, so it is not possible.

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. What is the probability of rolling a 4?
items.e: There are 6 equally likely outcomes and only one of them is 4: 16. 46 would be the chance of 1, 2, 3 or 4.

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. What is the probability of rolling an even number?
items.e: The even numbers are 2, 4 and 6: 3 of the 6 outcomes, so 36 (= 12). 63 is upside down: it is greater than 1.

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. What is the probability of rolling a number greater than 4?
items.e: Greater than 4 means 5 or 6: 2 of the 6 outcomes, so 26. 36 wrongly includes the 4. 16 forgets the 5.

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. What is the probability of rolling a number less than 5?
items.e: Less than 5 means 1, 2, 3 or 4: 4 of the 6 outcomes, so 46. 56 wrongly includes the 5. 26 counts the outcomes you don’t want (5 and 6).

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. What is the probability of rolling a multiple of 3?
items.e: The multiples of 3 on the cube are 3 and 6: 26. 36 also counts 9, which is not on the cube. 16 forgets the 6.

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. What is the probability of rolling a prime number?
items.e: The prime numbers are 2, 3 and 5: 36. 46 wrongly counts 1, which is not prime. 26 forgets that 2 is prime.

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. What is the probability of NOT rolling a 6?
items.e: Not a 6 means 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5: 56. Check: 56 + 16 = 1. 65 is upside down and greater than 1.

items.q: What is the probability of landing on red?
items.e: Red covers half of the spinner: 12. 13 counts the 3 colours, but the sections are not the same size.

items.q: The spinner has 8 equal sections: G is green and Y is yellow. What is the probability of green?
items.e: 3 of the 8 equal sections are green: 38. 35 compares green with yellow, not with all 8 sections. 58 is yellow.

items.q: A spinner has 10 equal sections: 3 blue and 7 red. What is the probability of blue as a decimal?
items.e: 3 of the 10 sections are blue: 310 = 0,3. 0,7 is the probability of red.

items.q: A bag has 3 red and 5 blue marbles. You take one without looking. What is the probability of red?
items.e: There are 3 + 5 = 8 marbles and 3 are red: 38. 35 compares red with blue, not with all the marbles. Two colours does not mean 12.

items.q: You take one marble without looking. What is the probability of blue?
items.e: There are 4 + 2 + 2 = 8 marbles and 2 are blue: 28 (= 14). 26 compares blue with the other 6 marbles, not with all 8. 48 is red.

items.q: A bag has 20 marbles and 5 of them are green. What is the probability of green as a percent?
items.e: 520 = 25100 = 25%. 5% uses the number of green marbles as the percent. 75% is NOT green.

items.q: A bag has 3 red and 7 yellow marbles. What is the probability of NOT getting red?
items.e: Not red means yellow: 7 of the 10 marbles, so 710. Check: 310 + 710 = 1.

items.q: Cards numbered 1 to 10 are shuffled. You pick one. What is the probability of a multiple of 3?
items.e: The multiples of 3 are 3, 6 and 9: 3 of the 10 cards, so 310. 13 comes from the word “3”, not from counting cards.

items.q: What is the probability of landing on a prime number?
items.e: The prime numbers are 2, 3, 5 and 7: 4 of the 8 sections, so 48 (= 12). 58 wrongly counts 1, which is not prime. 38 forgets 2.

items.q: A bag has 2 red, 3 blue and 5 green marbles. What is the probability of red or blue?
items.e: Red or blue: 2 + 3 = 5 of the 10 marbles, so 510. 55 compares red and blue with green; it would mean certain.

items.q: Red is in two small parts, each one eighth of the spinner. What is the probability of red?
items.e: 18 + 18 = 28 = 14. 25 counts 2 of the 5 sections, but the sections are not the same size.

items.q: The letters of TORONTO are written on 7 cards. You pick one card without looking. What is the probability of O?
items.e: TORONTO has 7 letters and 3 of them are O: 37. 14 counts the 4 different letters, but O is on 3 cards. 34 compares the 3 O cards with the other 4 cards.

items.q: A 12-sided die has the numbers 1 to 12. What is the probability of rolling a number greater than 9, as a percent?
items.e: Greater than 9 means 10, 11 or 12: 312 = 14 = 25%. 3% uses the count as the percent.

items.q: The probability of heads is 12. What is this as a decimal?
items.e: 12 = 1 ÷ 2 = 0,5. Writing the digits 1 and 2 as 0,12 or 1,2 is a common mistake.

items.q: The probability of landing on blue is 14. What is this as a percentage?
items.e: 14 = 25100 = 25%. 14% just writes the digits 1 and 4.

items.q: Write the probability 310 as a decimal.
items.e: 310 is 3 tenths = 0,3. 0,03 is 3 hundredths.

items.q: Write the probability 0,75 as a percentage.
items.e: To change a decimal to a percentage, multiply by 100: 0,75 × 100 = 75%.

items.q: Which fraction is equal to the probability 0,2?
items.e: 0,2 = 210 = 15. 12 is 0,5, and 2100 is 0,02.

items.q: Write the probability 15 as a percentage.
items.e: 15 = 20100 = 20%. Multiply the top and bottom by 20.

items.q: Write the probability 910 as a decimal.
items.e: 910 is 9 tenths = 0,9. 0,1 is the probability that the event does NOT happen.

items.q: Write the probability 35 as a percentage.
items.e: 35 = 60100 = 60%. Multiply the top and bottom by 20.

items.q: Write the probability 40% as a fraction in simplest form.
items.e: 40% = 40100. Divide the top and bottom by 20: 25. 4100 would be 4%.

items.q: Write the probability 0,05 as a percentage.
You roll a six-sided dice. What is the probability of rolling a 4?
items.e: There are 6 equally likely outcomes and only one of them is 4: 16. 46 would be the chance of 1, 2, 3 or 4.

items.q: You roll a six-sided dice. What is the probability of rolling an even number?
items.e: The even numbers are 2, 4 and 6: 3 of the 6 outcomes, so 36 (= 12). 63 is upside down: it is bigger than 1.

items.q: You roll a six-sided dice. What is the probability of rolling a number greater than 4?
items.e: Greater than 4 means 5 or 6: 2 of the 6 outcomes, so 26. 36 wrongly includes the 4. 16 forgets the 5.

items.q: A bag has 20 marbles and 5 of them are green. What is the probability of green as a percentage?
items.e: 520 = 25100 = 25%. 5% uses the number of green marbles as the percentage. 75% is NOT green.

items.q: The letters of AUSTRALIA are written on 9 cards. You pick one card. What is the probability of A?
items.e: AUSTRALIA has 9 letters and 3 of them are A: 39. 17 counts the 7 different letters, but A is on 3 cards.

items.q: A 12-sided dice has the numbers 1 to 12. What is the probability of rolling a number greater than 9, as a percentage?
items.e: Greater than 9 means 10, 11 or 12: 312 = 14 = 25%. 3% uses the count as the percentage.

items.q: On which spinner is the probability of blue 14?
items.e: On spinner C blue has 2 of the 8 equal sections: 28 = 14. A has 4 sections, but blue is half of it.

items.q: Which bag gives a probability of 0,5 for taking a red marble?
items.e: 0,5 means half of the marbles are red. With 4 red and 4 blue, 4 of 8 are red. 5 red, 10 blue gives 515, not 510.

items.q: A bag has 10 marbles. The probability of red is 25. How many red marbles are there?
items.e: 25 = 410, so 4 of the 10 marbles are red. 2 uses the top number without changing to tenths. 6 is the number that are not red.

items.q: A bag has 3 green marbles and some blue marbles. The probability of green is 14. How many blue marbles are there?
items.e: 14 = 312, so there are 12 marbles in total. 12 − 3 = 9 blue. 12 is the total, not the number of blue marbles.

items.q: You roll a fair dice 60 times. About how many times would you expect to roll a 6?
items.e: A 6 has probability 16. 16 of 60 is 60 ÷ 6 = 10, so about 10.

items.q: You toss a fair coin 100 times. How many heads would you expect?
items.e: Half of 100 is 50. Results change from one experiment to the next, so expect about 50, not exactly 50.

items.q: You spin this spinner 40 times. About how many times would you expect red?
items.e: Red is 34 of the spinner. 40 ÷ 4 = 10, and 3 × 10 = 30, so about 30. About 10 is for blue.

items.q: Pieter tosses a coin 50 times and gets 23 heads. What is the experimental probability of heads?
items.e: Experimental probability = times it happened ÷ number of trials = 2350. 12 is the theoretical probability. 2327 compares heads with tails.

items.q: What is the experimental probability of red, as a decimal?
items.e: Red came up 12 times in 20 spins: 1220 = 610 = 0,6. 1,5 comes from 12 ÷ 8 (red ÷ blue), and it is bigger than 1.

items.q: What is the experimental probability of yellow, as a percentage?
items.e: Yellow came up 10 times in 40 spins: 1040 = 14 = 25%. 10% uses the count as the percentage.

items.q: Palesa spins a spinner 50 times and gets blue 18 times. What is the experimental probability of blue, as a percentage?
items.e: 1850 = 36100 = 36%. 32% comes from 50 − 18. 64% is NOT blue.

items.q: A fair coin lands on tails 5 times in a row. What is the probability of heads on the next toss?
items.e: The coin has no memory. Every toss is a new trial, so heads is still 12. Thinking heads is “due” is called the gambler’s fallacy.

items.q: Ethan has rolled a fair dice 12 times without getting a 6. What is the probability of a 6 on the next roll?
items.e: The dice does not remember earlier rolls. A 6 is still 16. It is not certain (1), even after a long wait.

items.q: Lerato tosses a coin 10 times and gets 7 heads. Liam tosses a coin 1 000 times and gets 508 heads. Whose experimental probability of heads is closer to 12?
items.e: Lerato: 710 = 0,7. Liam: 5081 000 = 0,508. 0,508 is much closer to 0,5, so Liam’s is closer.

items.q: Daniel tosses a coin 50 times and gets 23 heads. What is the experimental probability of heads?
items.e: Experimental probability = number of times it happened ÷ number of trials = 2350. 12 is the theoretical probability. 2327 compares heads with tails.

items.q: Which sentence describes experimental probability?
c: The number of times it happened
The number of trials ÷ the number of times it happened
The outcomes you want ÷ all the possible outcomes
The number of times it happened ÷ the number of trials
items.e: Experimental probability comes from what happened in an experiment: times it happened ÷ number of trials. Counting the possible outcomes gives the theoretical probability.

items.q: Nadia’s class recorded 20 spins. What is the experimental probability of red, as a decimal?
items.e: Red came up 12 times in 20 spins: 1220 = 610 = 0,6. 1,5 comes from 12 ÷ 8 (red ÷ blue), and it is greater than 1.

items.q: What is the experimental probability of yellow, as a percent?
items.e: Yellow came up 10 times in 40 spins: 1040 = 14 = 25%. 10% uses the count as the percent. 30% is blue.

items.q: What is the experimental probability of rolling a 4?
items.e: The tally for 4 shows 3 rolls out of 30: 330. 16 is the theoretical probability. 430 uses the number 4 instead of its frequency.

items.q: Ethan takes a marble from a bag, records its colour and puts it back. He does this 50 times. What is the experimental probability of NOT red?
items.e: Not red means blue or green: 18 + 10 = 28 of the 50 draws, so 2850. 2250 is red. 1050 counts only green.

items.q: Ravi flips a bottle cap 80 times. It lands top-up 36 times. What is the experimental probability of top-up, as a percent?
items.e: 3680 = 920 = 45100 = 45%. 36% uses the count as the percent. 55% is top-down. 44% comes from 80 − 36.

items.q: Chloe spins a spinner 25 times and gets green 9 times. What is the experimental probability of green, as a decimal?
items.e: 925 = 36100 = 0,36. 0,09 and 0,9 just use the 9. 0,64 is the probability of NOT green.

items.q: Megan takes 15 penalty kicks at soccer practice and scores 6 times. What is her experimental probability of scoring, as a decimal?
items.e: 615 = 25 = 0,4. 0,6 is the kicks she missed. 0,06 uses the count as the decimal.

items.q: What is the experimental probability of blue or green?
items.e: Blue or green: 11 + 8 = 19 of the 30 spins, so 1930. 24 counts 2 of the 4 colours, but experimental probability uses the results.

items.q: Liam and Elna toss a coin. Liam wins on heads and Elna wins on tails. Is the game fair?
c: No, Liam is more likely to win
No, Elna is more likely to win
Yes, each has a probability of 12
items.e: A game is fair when every player has the same probability of winning. Heads and tails are both 12, so yes.

items.q: Sibusiso and Chloe roll a number cube. Sibusiso wins on 1 or 2. Chloe wins on 3, 4, 5 or 6. Is the game fair?
c: No, Sibusiso is more likely to win
Yes, they each have a number
No, Chloe is more likely to win
Yes, each has 12
items.e: Sibusiso: 26. Chloe: 46. The chances are not equal, so no, Chloe is more likely to win.

items.q: Dumisani and Lerato roll a number cube. Dumisani wins on an even number and Lerato wins on an odd number. What is Lerato’s probability of winning?
items.e: The odd numbers are 1, 3 and 5: 36. Dumisani also has 36 (2, 4, 6), so the game is fair. 33 compares Lerato’s numbers with Dumisani’s.

items.q: Ayanda and Thabo roll a number cube. Ayanda wins on a prime number. Thabo wins on a number that is not prime. What is Thabo’s probability of winning?
items.e: Not prime: 1, 4 and 6 (1 is not a prime number). That is 36. 26 forgets the 1. 46 thinks 2 is not prime. So the game is fair.

items.q: Ethan wins if the spinner lands on red. Palesa wins if it lands on blue or yellow. Is the game fair?
c: No, Palesa has 23
Yes, each has 12
No, Ethan is more likely to win
items.e: Ethan: red = 12. Palesa: 14 + 14 = 12. Yes, it is fair. Counting colours (1 against 2) is the mistake.

items.q: Ravi wins on red, Megan wins on blue and Daniel wins on yellow. Who is most likely to win?
items.e: Ravi’s red is 12 of the spinner. Megan and Daniel have 14 each. Ravi is most likely to win, so the game is not fair.

items.q: Pieter, Anika and Dumisani roll a number cube. Pieter wins on 1 or 2, Anika on 3 or 4, and Dumisani on 5 or 6. What is each player’s probability of winning?
items.e: Each player has 2 of the 6 numbers: 26 (= 13). The three chances are equal, so the game is fair.

items.q: A spinner has 8 equal sections: 5 blue and 3 red. Ethan wins on blue and Sarah wins on red. Which change makes the game fair?
items.e: A fair spinner needs 4 blue and 4 red sections. Painting 1 blue section red gives 48 each. Painting 2 would give 3 blue and 5 red: unfair the other way.

items.q: A bag has 4 green and 6 yellow marbles. Palesa wins if she takes a green marble. What is her probability of winning?
items.e: 4 of the 10 marbles are green: 410. 46 compares green with yellow. 12 counts 2 colours, but there are more yellow marbles.

items.q: The bag has 4 green and 6 yellow marbles. Palesa wins on green and Thabo wins on yellow. How many green marbles should be added to make the game fair?
items.e: Fair means the same number of green and yellow marbles: 6 green and 6 yellow. 6 − 4 = 2. Adding 6 would make 10 green. 1 would only work if you also took out a yellow one.

items.q: There is a 70% chance of rain tomorrow. What is the chance that it does NOT rain?
items.e: Rain and no rain add up to 100%. 100% − 70% = 30%. It is not 0%, because 70% is not certain.

items.q: The forecast said a 70% chance of rain, but it stayed dry all day. Was the forecast wrong?
items.e: 70% means rain is likely, but there was still a 30% chance of no rain. A dry day does not make the forecast wrong: 70% is likely, not certain.

items.q: The Grade 6 raffle sells 100 tickets and one ticket wins. Precious buys 4 tickets. What is her probability of winning, as a decimal?
items.e: 4100 = 0,04. 0,25 is 14, which mixes up the 4 tickets with quarters. 0,96 is the chance she does NOT win.

items.q: Precious has 4 of the 100 raffle tickets. What is the probability that she does NOT win, as a percentage?
items.e: 96 of the 100 tickets are not hers: 96100 = 96%. 4% is her chance of winning.

items.q: A raffle at the school fete sells 200 tickets. Kabelo buys 5. What is his probability of winning, as a percentage?
items.e: 5200 = 140 = 0,025 = 2,5%. 5% would be 5 out of 100, but there are 200 tickets.

items.q: Raffle tickets are numbered 1 to 200. What is the probability that the winning ticket ends in 7?
items.e: 7, 17, 27, … 197: that is 20 tickets. 20200 = 110 = 10%. 20% uses the count as the percentage.

items.q: At the fundraiser, 10 of the 40 sausages are vegetarian. Thabo gets one at random. What is the probability it is vegetarian?
items.e: 1040 = 14. 13 compares 10 vegetarian with the 30 others, not with all 40.

items.q: At the swimming gala, 20 of the first 50 learners Lwazi saw were wearing a hat. Estimate the probability that the next learner wears a hat.
items.e: 2050 = 410 = 0,4. 2,5 comes from 50 ÷ 20, and it is bigger than 1.

items.q: A bag has 5 red and 5 blue marbles. Lerato takes a red one and does NOT put it back. What is the probability that the next marble is red?
items.e: Now there are 4 red and 5 blue: 9 marbles left. So the probability is 49. 410 forgets that the bag now has 9 marbles.

items.q: A raffle has 300 tickets. How many tickets must Zinhle buy to have a 10% chance of winning?
items.e: 10% of 300 = 300 ÷ 10 = 30. Buying 10 tickets gives only 10300, about 3%.
